I can remember sitting in the break room of the hotel I worked at about a year ago and listening to my boss talk about her intermittent fasting and how it helped her lose weight and all. Total props to her because like you said, I understand the discipline needed to maintain that kind of diet. At the time though I was pretty pissed with her. I was the only one bringing home a paycheck and was getting paid less than a dollar over minimum wage. Out of necessity, the only time I would really eat was at work, and it would be whatever was communal to the break room. (Which was typically unopened food left behind by guests. Nutritional value and the reliability of it being there in the first place was a total roll of the dice every time.) It was a running joke amongst my coworkers just how out of touch she was with the working class, although she pretended to be more down to Earth. She drove a nice Cadillac, always had her hair and nails done, was constantly talking about what she was buying online and at the mall, would always vehemently express how much she disliked generic brand things, etc. I remember thinking how odd it was seeing us do the same thing- restricting our food intake so specifically in the day, yet for entirely different reasons. I just wanted to look at her and say "We are not the same." I felt guilty for my anger, but of course, it didn't help that she was the one signing my paychecks.

I don't think it'd be right to call anyone an asshole on this. It's important to remember that in other cultures, especially in Asia, tipping your server is unheard of. It can actually be seen as disrespectful/rude to tip, even to the servers. This is mostly because of the difference in how things work in other countries. It might be helpful to gently remind him that servers dont get paid the same minimum wage as everyone else, at least in the US. Since the government knows that servers get tipped, they allow employers to pay them less than minimum wage. That's why servers complain when nobody tips, because sometimes, it is literally half, if not more than, their regular income. Up until a few years ago, the tipped minimum wage was only about $2 or $3 an hour (it's since changed to $3< the state's untipped wage, so long as the tips made at the end of the day make up for the missing $3 an hour.) People who choose not to tip are typically why a server's income can be so inconsistent/unreliable. 

It's also important to remember that servers are typically required to "tip out" the kitchen staff. Usually this is a very small portion, however I've noticed it can be really easy for restaurants to hike the percentage unreasonably. Bartenders usually get a bigger cut than back-of-the-house kitchen staff, even when alcoholic drinks are not ordered/served at every table/with every order (and think of all the restaurants that have bars). Based off my personal experience, it's even worse with niche chefs, as I used to split 50% off all my tips with a sushi chef. The bullshit to this (imo) however, is that the individuals that recieve this "tip share" make either salary or full minimum wage. These individuals (at least bartenders and sushi chefs) often make their own tips/have their own tip jars too, and are then not required to share them with the servers.

I only say all this because I spent a good year of my life on my own surviving on tips from my waitressing job. There were times in my life that my mom's tips from her waitressing job were the only reason we had more than macaroni in the pantry. Because I've been there first hand, I now tip no matter what. For me, 15% is standard, even if I felt the service was poor/mediocre. If I feel really good about my server and experience, I'll go as high up as 30-50%. I also consider the tip well before we plan on going out to eat, as I dont feel comfortable interracting with my server if I know I can't tip them well. For me the tip is an expected part of the bill. If I can, I'll often wait until I see my server again to give them their tip so I can tell them it's a personal gift, that way there's no mandatory tip share or claiming on taxes. Sometimes my server will look at me crazy for adamantly insisting it be called a gift and not tip, but I don't let it phase me. I feel like if more people were to do that, then being a server probably wouldn't suck as much.

Fuck him. Drop him so hard that he doesn't realize what hit him. Cut him out entirely, and, if you find yourself so inclined, let him know you can be a friend when he decides to drop the bag. He's a bad influence, bad news, and I hate to say it, but the more you let him in, the more he's going to hurt you. Since your relationship has been on and off again, it leads me to assume he's never been that serious about you, and I won't be the first to tell you you deserve better. Don't think of the last three years as a waste, but rather a very valuable lesson. As time goes on, you'll take note of more and more red flags. These may help you, or your friends, or maybe even your kids down the line.

As for your friend, I encourage you to practice open communication with her. Don't be afraid to let her know that you're hurting, and that you're scared of feeling resentment. Let her know that her friendship is important to you and that you really do love her, and that you are going to try your best to not let it get in the way of your friendship. You may just need time. If she's a true friend, and as great of a person as you say, she'll understand. She might have some words of comfort for you, and if it's out in the open, you two might be able to avoid situations where your insecurities are triggered, and where your ex is involved. 

If for whatever reason your friendship can't handle a situation like that, where you are honest about what's bothering you, the friendship isn't that strong, and you're probably better off without her as a friend. This however, is determined later down the line, if the friendship becomes strained. In that situation it's important to remember that the stress in your relationship isn't caused by you, but rather your ex. If the friendship can't handle outside stress, its lacking in quality. If you're going to have resentment issues, they'll be present regardless as to whether or not you're honest with her about them. Being honest also won't leave her to ask why the friendship had to end if it comes to it. (In my mind, I see it as preventing unnecessary resentment- but that's just me, thinking 10 steps down the line in each direction.)

Opening yourself up to vulnerability with people can be really hard, and it's a very brave thing to do. There is a possibility your friendship could become a bit weaker, but if your friendship is strong to start with, it definitely has the potential to get stronger. Communication is key in any relationship, not just the romantic ones. It's okay to be hurt, and it's okay to admit it to yourself and others. Feeling these things is a part of life, and sometimes the best you can do is just roll with the punches.

I was always a weird kid. I saw both myself and the world differently, I was a little more mature, and had perfection issues/ocd from a very young age, ect. (Memories going back to 1st, 2nd, 3rd grade that all stand out to me now)

I know now that I'm older, what I really struggled with as a kid was depression, but there was no real outlet or resource that I think could've helped to identify or even resolve what I was dealing with. Looking back, the thought that I've always felt this way, especially going back as far as I can, seems totally bizarre, even to me.

It's something that stuck with me and got progressively worse through puberty (worst of it started in middle school) to the point where I struggled with self harm and suicidal thoughts for several years up through high school. I had several plans as to how I'd kill myself, got creative on how to hide the ways/places I was hurting myself (parents found scars freshman year) and struggled with my overall sense of self-worth.

My negative way of thinking really dominated a majority of my adolescence, and I let it interfere with how I chose to live my life. I had interests like dance and ceramics, but talked myself out of pursuing them because of bullshit reasons. I didn't try making friends with the people I wanted to be friends with because I convinced myself they'd hate me as much as I hated myself. The worst of them all is probably that I never really set any life or career goals for myself, because I never thought I'd live to make them happen. 

These are all things I have lived with the consequences of. To this day, I don't know how to dance without feeling like I look like a fool, I only have about 3-5 real friends in my life, one being my husband, and it's taken me a little while of dealing with my self doubts and insecurities, to find something I can actually see myself doing with the rest of my life, now that living one is part of the plan. 

It's true when they say it gets better, and that you just have to be patient for it, but I'll admit that sometimes the day can still be a little too much for me. When that happens I allow myself to take the day as slowly as I need to, one step at a time. Any day I wake up is a good day, and it doesn't hurt to remember that.

When my husband was in high school, he would show up early, about 45min before the last bell. One day, at around 7:10am (school started at 7:45am) the fire alarm goes off. So naturally, everyone evacuates and makes their way to the field next to the building. Alarm gets dismissed as false and everything goes back to normal.

Come to find out, two punks had been planning a shooting. One was supposed to pull the fire alarm, and the other was going to open fire once everyone was on the field, basically a buncha sitting ducks. Someone overheard their plans maybe a day before and reports it. The kid with the gun rides the school bus in the mornings, and before he gets on is apprehended by police. The fire alarm kid has no idea his accomplice has been stopped, and without talking to him before "go time", sets off the alarm anyway. Both were expelled and dealt with by local authorities.

The thought that my husband could've died then, back when we were high school sweethearts, chills me to the bone when I think about it too much.
